design_detail: Analysis of an international online survey of people who had drunk ayahuasca at least once, run 2017 to 2019 in English, Portuguese, Spanish, German, Italian and Czech, with non-random recruitment through organizations, retreat centres, ayahuasca churches, online groups and forums, Facebook and conference flyers, no incentive, and University of Melbourne ethics approval (1545143.3). Of 10,836 respondents, the 6,877 who had drunk ayahuasca with two or fewer groups were analysed. Exposures, all self-reported: context of the last drink (ayahuasca church, traditional shaman, or other); motivations (15 checkboxes in three factor scores); ceremony characteristics present in the last context (counts of traditional and non-traditional practices; religious hymns or sermons); a 1 to 4 rating of support and safety and a 1 to 4 rating of preparation activities; additional supports offered outside ceremonies at the place of drinking (religious or spiritual counselling, psychologist or psychotherapist, yoga or tai-chi, fasting); and drinking mostly in a traditional Amazonian country other than Brazil. Outcomes: intermediate (self-insights, Short Index of Mystical Orientation, a single spiritual-significance item, extreme fear or panic during a session, integration difficulties in the weeks or months after, closeness of a drinking community) and final (perceived growth in psychological wellbeing, SF-12 mental component score, Kessler-10, and, for 1,278 people with anxiety or depression diagnosed when they drank, the Patient Global Impression of Change). Linear and stereotype logistic regressions after multiple imputation (20 data sets), adjusted for age, sex, university education, number of lifetime mental-health diagnoses, number of times drunk and years since the last drink, then a generalized structural equation model built iteratively on the same data. Rated with ROBINS-E.
can_establish: How ceremony practices, support and preparation ratings, additional supports and motivations differed between church, traditional-shaman and other contexts among 6,877 self-selected people who drink ayahuasca, and which of them went with these people's retrospective ratings of the acute experience and of later difficulties, and with their current mental health, after adjustment for a few demographic and drinking-history variables.
cannot_establish: That any ceremony feature, support, preparation activity or fasting changes the acute experience or mental health (one cross-sectional, self-selected, self-report survey with no measure taken before ayahuasca, exposures rated retrospectively by the people who rated the outcomes, and a path model selected on the same data); the dose, composition or purity of what was drunk (not measured); or how often frightening experiences or later difficulties occur among people who drink ayahuasca generally.

sample.recruitment: Online survey 2017 to 2019 in six languages, promoted through websites and email invitations from relevant organizations, ayahuasca retreat centres and churches, online groups and forums, Facebook, and flyers at conferences and events; no financial incentive; suspected duplicates removed and partly completed surveys kept (Materials and Methods › Study Design, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18 or over, with at least one use of ayahuasca. For this paper only respondents who had drunk with two or fewer groups were included (6,877 of 10,836); the reason for the restriction is not stated.
sample.demographics: By last context (church, traditional, other; Table 3): women 50.7%, 48.5%, 50.6%; mean age 40.0, 40.3 and 38.4 years; university education 63.2%, 60.4%, 61.3%; living in Brazil 87.0%, 6.4%, 19.4%, in Europe 4.8%, 41.5%, 41.0%, in North America 6.8%, 31.9%, 22.2%; any lifetime mental-health diagnosis 29.2%, 39.0%, 44.5%; ayahuasca drunk more than 200 times 56.8%, 0.3%, 1.1%, and 5 times or fewer 7.1%, 66.0%, 68.0% (editors' sums of Table 3 rows); years since the last drink 1.2, 1.6 and 1.2.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single survey). Item non-response is visible in Table 3 (for example, lifetime mental-health diagnoses answered by 5,524 of the 6,817 with a known context) and was handled by multiple imputation; the amount missing per variable is not otherwise reported.
sample.selection_effects: Non-random, self-selected sample recruited largely through ayahuasca organizations, retreat centres and churches; the authors state that it risks a bias towards people who had positive effects (Discussion, 8th paragraph). People who were harmed or who stopped drinking may be under-represented. The unexplained restriction to people who drank with two or fewer groups removed 37% of respondents (editors' calculation). Church members are half of the sample and differ sharply from the others in country, number of times drunk and mental-health history.

exposure.measurement: All self-reported in one online survey. Context of the last drink: a ceremony with one or more traditional shamans; the UDV, Santo Daime or Barquinha churches; or other (non-traditional, mixed, no guide or no ceremony). Motivations: 15 checkboxes summed in three factors from an exploratory factor analysis, therapeutic (0 to 6), self-knowledge (0 to 4) and experiential (0 to 5). Ceremony characteristics present in the last context: traditional (0 to 6: live icaros, recommended sexual abstinence before ceremonies, blowing of smoke, individual blessings, whistling, sucking from affected parts of the body), non-traditional (0 to 5: smudging, other live singing, non-traditional instruments, recitations, dance) and religious hymns or sermons (yes or no). Two ratings of the respondent's experience of the last context, 1 (not at all) to 4 (very much): support and safety (mean of 4 items: empathy, respect and genuineness of those leading; emotional and physical safety in the ceremony space; availability of support during the ceremony; a sense of the ceremony as a powerful and sacred ritual) and preparation activities (mean of 2 items: a chance to discuss one's history, motivations or concerns before drinking; guidance before drinking about dealing with possible difficulties). Additional supports provided outside ceremonies at the place of drinking (yes or no): religious or spiritual counselling, a psychologist or psychotherapist session, yoga or tai-chi, fasting. Most drinking in Peru, Colombia, Ecuador, Bolivia or Venezuela (Brazil excluded) coded as a traditional country.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Dose, concentration, quantity and composition of the brew were not measured (Discussion, 8th paragraph). Lifetime number of times drunk was recorded in 10 categories (from 1 to 500–5000) and entered as a covariate, as were years since the last drink.
exposure.polysubstance: Not measured or adjusted in this paper; alcohol and other drug use from the same survey is analysed in a companion paper (Perkins et al., 2021, cited for the list of self-insights).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. Current mental health (SF-12, K10) was measured at the survey, a mean of 1.2 to 1.6 years after the last drink (Table 3).

comparison.controls: No group without ayahuasca. Comparisons are among people who drink ayahuasca: across contexts and regions (Tables 2 and 3), and by levels of each motivation, ceremony, support and country variable, each adjusted for the others and for the covariates (Tables 4 and 5).
comparison.matching: None; regression adjustment for age (decades), sex, university education, number of lifetime mental-health diagnoses, number of times drunk (the category entered as a single term) and years since the last drink, with all exposure variables entered together.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Mental health before any ayahuasca use (proxied only by the number of lifetime diagnoses, whose timing relative to ayahuasca is unknown; the authors call the proxy not completely satisfactory), personality, state of mind when drinking (the authors note that set was limited to motivations), dose and composition, other drug use, and the facilitators' skill (proxied by country).

outcomes.instruments: Intermediate: number of self-insights (7 listed insights, alpha 0.80); the Short Index of Mystical Orientation (9 items rated 1 to 10, total 9 to 90, with 'god' replaced by 'god/spirit/the divine'), used for the intensity of mystical experience during the acute phase; the spirituality item of the Persisting Effects Questionnaire (PEQ-S: one six-point item, from not at all significant to the single most spiritually significant experience of one's life); extreme fear or panic during the ayahuasca session (one item, 0 to 10); number of integration difficulties in the weeks or months after drinking (PHQ-4 plus 5 items such as feeling disconnected or alone, or disturbing thoughts, feelings or sensations); closeness of a community one drinks with (4 points). Final: perceived growth in psychological wellbeing (PWG; Psychological Well-Being Post-Traumatic Changes Questionnaire, 18 items on 5 points); SF-12 mental component score (0 to 100, higher better) and Kessler-10 (10 to 50, higher more distress), both current; the Patient Global Impression of Change (6 points, from much worsened to completely improved) for anxiety or depression diagnosed when drinking ayahuasca on any occasion.
outcomes.validity_norms: SF-12 and K10 are standard measures of current status and, as the authors note, not retrospective. The PWB-PTCQ was developed for change after trauma. The Short Index of Mystical Orientation's source, by the title in the reference list, is a study of mystical orientation among Roman Catholic priests, and no validation for rating an acute ayahuasca experience is reported. The spirituality, fear and community measures are single items and the self-insight and integration counts are new; no validation is reported for them.
outcomes.operationalization: A difficult experience is extreme fear or panic during a session (one item) and integration difficulties in the weeks or months after; a good one is self-insights, mystical and spiritual ratings and community closeness. All were rated by the respondent at the survey, retrospectively, for an occasion that is not always specified (the exposures refer to the last context); none was measured before drinking. Which outcomes were modelled by stereotype logistic rather than linear regression is not stated.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 130 counts the coefficients of the 13 non-covariate predictors across the 6 intermediate (Table 4) and 4 final (Table 5) outcomes; Table 2 adds 30 tests of differences by context and region, and the path model further tests.

analysis.effect_sizes: Unstandardized coefficients B (SE) with p values; no R-squared, standardized coefficients or intervals (the 95% intervals below are B ± 1.96 SE, editors' calculation). Support and safety (1 to 4): extreme fear −0.29 (−0.43 to −0.15), integration difficulties −0.13 (−0.23 to −0.03), K10 −0.62 (−0.86 to −0.38), SF-12 MCS 1.5 (1.05 to 1.95), PWG 1.91 (1.42 to 2.40), SIMO 2.42 (1.60 to 3.24), PGIC 0.07 (p = 0.181). Preparation activities (1 to 4): integration difficulties −0.14 (−0.20 to −0.08), extreme fear −0.01 (p = 0.816), K10 −0.25 (−0.39 to −0.11), SF-12 MCS 0.45 (0.18 to 0.72), PWG 0.75 (0.48 to 1.02), PGIC 0.13 (0.07 to 0.19). Fasting: SIMO 1.69 (0.44 to 2.94), PWG 0.97 (0.24 to 1.70), no other association. Traditional practices: extreme fear 0.18 (0.12 to 0.24), K10 0.16 (0.04 to 0.28). Drinking mostly in a traditional country: extreme fear 0.7 (0.43 to 0.97), K10 −0.47 (−0.90 to −0.04). Religious characteristics: extreme fear −0.38 (−0.56 to −0.20). Therapeutic motivation: extreme fear 0.21 (0.15 to 0.27), integration difficulties 0.15 (0.11 to 0.19), K10 0.43 (0.33 to 0.53). For scale: across the whole 1 to 4 range of either rating, the adjusted difference in current distress is under 2 points of the K10's 40-point span (editors' arithmetic). Path coefficients of the structural model are only in Figure 2 (an image) and supplementary Table S1 (not read).
analysis.covariates: Age (decades), female sex, university education, number of lifetime mental-health diagnoses, number of times drunk and years since the last drink; all exposures entered together; multiple imputation by chained equations (20 data sets) for all model variables; multicollinearity checked (VIF above 3, correlations above 0.7: none).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned. The structural model was selected by iteratively adding or removing paths using the regression results, theoretical justification, path significance and information criteria (Materials and Methods › Statistical Analysis, 3rd paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Tables 4 and 5 print every coefficient, which limits selective reporting within the regressions. The structural model, selected on the same data, is presented in the abstract as verifying the relationships. The discussion's summaries depart from the tables in two places (reporting issue 4).
analysis.power: Not addressed. With 6,877 respondents very small coefficients reach significance; the authors note that many effects were small individually (Discussion, 3rd paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among self-selected people who drink ayahuasca, half of them church members mostly in Brazil and most of the rest people who had drunk a few times in traditional or other contexts, higher ratings of support and safety at the last ceremony, and of preparation activities, went with fewer reported integration difficulties, more self-insights and higher spiritual ratings, more perceived growth in wellbeing and slightly better current mental health; support and safety, but not preparation, also went with less reported extreme fear. Traditional practices, drinking mostly in a traditional Amazonian country, non-traditional practices and therapeutic motivation went with more reported extreme fear, and religious church characteristics with less. Fasting and yoga or tai-chi went with higher mystical and wellbeing-growth ratings. The adjusted differences are small: under 2 K10 points across the full range of either rating.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says a structural model was used to verify the relationships, the methods describe that model as a network of causal relationships, and the conclusion states that aspects of setting and set "appear to have significant effects" on acute experiences, integration difficulties and longer-term mental health (Discussion, 10th paragraph), singling out supports giving a sense of safety and preparation activities as especially important. Gaps: (1) causal and verification language from one cross-sectional survey, with a path model chosen on the same data; (2) the support-and-safety rating is the respondent's own retrospective judgment of the ceremony, near the top of its scale (means 3.4 to 3.9 of 4), and contains items close to the outcomes (feeling safe in the ceremony space versus extreme fear; a powerful and sacred ritual versus spiritual significance), so the association can run from the experience to the rating; (3) there is no measure of mental health before ayahuasca and no dose information, both acknowledged; (4) the discussion overstates two table results (reporting issue 4). Against this, the authors state the main limitations (self-selection favouring positive experiences, self-report, retrospective items, no pre-use mental health, no dose data), note that many effects were small, and conclude that no one set of practices was shown to be superior.

replication.where_it_stands: No independent replication. Companion and later papers from overlapping authors appear to draw on the same survey and must not be counted as independent support. Studies of set and setting in ayahuasca ceremonies and retreats on this project's DMT-Ayahuasca list (Uthaug et al., 2021; Pontual et al., 2022), not read for this card, are the next comparisons; the question whether support, preparation or fasting changes the experience needs measures taken before and soon after ceremonies.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study of people booked into ayahuasca ceremonies of different kinds that measures mental health, expectations and state of mind before the ceremony, records what was drunk where possible, has setting and support rated independently by observers as well as by participants, and rates the acute experience (fear, challenging and mystical experience) within a day and mental health at follow-up, against pre-specified hypotheses; where retreats already differ in preparation, a cluster-randomized comparison of a standard preparation session would test preparation directly.

domains.note: Adjusted for age, sex, education, number of lifetime diagnoses, number of times drunk and years since the last drink, but not for mental health before ayahuasca, personality, state of mind, dose or other drug use; number of times drunk, entered as one term across ten categories, cannot remove the very large difference in experience between church members and the others.

For the support-and-safety and preparation ratings, the exposures the paper emphasizes: retrospective self-ratings of the last ceremony, near the ceiling, with items overlapping the outcomes in content and open to being shaped by how the experience went. The yes-or-no supports (fasting, yoga, counselling) are less exposed to this and would be judged high. Exposures refer to the last context, while several outcomes refer to unspecified or earlier occasions; motivations have no stated reference time.

Self-selected through organizations, retreat centres and churches, with a likely bias towards positive experiences that the authors acknowledge; 37% of respondents removed by an unexplained restriction to two or fewer groups.

Later ceremonies, integration work and therapy between the last drink and the survey (a mean of 1.2 to 1.6 years) are not recorded; the number of times drunk, adjusted for, is partly a consequence of earlier experiences.

Multiple imputation (20 data sets) for all model variables, outcomes included, with partly completed surveys kept; the amount missing per variable and the missing-at-random assumption are not reported or discussed.

Most outcomes are retrospective self-ratings by the person who rated the exposures, several of them single items or unvalidated counts; the SF-12 and K10 are current and validated, which lowers the concern for those two.

All regression coefficients are printed, but there is no registration, about 130 coefficient tests without correction, and a path model selected by significance and information criteria on the same data.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As evidence that support, preparation, ceremony features or fasting change the ayahuasca experience or mental health, the associations are at very high risk of bias: the central exposures are retrospective ratings of the respondent's own ceremony that overlap in content with the outcomes and can be shaped by them, the sample is self-selected through the organizations whose ceremonies are being rated, and nothing was measured before ayahuasca. The yes-or-no supports and the current mental-health measures (SF-12, K10) are less affected, but their associations remain confounded and small. Cite the paper for what this large self-selected sample reported about ceremony practices, supports and fasting in different contexts (Tables 1 to 3), and, labelled as cross-sectional and self-rated, for the pattern that feeling safe and supported and being offered preparation went with fewer reported difficulties and slightly better current mental health, and that traditional practices, drinking in traditional countries and therapeutic motivation went with more reported extreme fear. Do not cite it for any practice causing or preventing difficult experiences, for the path model as a causal or verified structure, or for effect sizes as clinically meaningful.

design_detail: Anonymous online cross-sectional survey (Qualtrics), February–December 2018, of adults who reported at least one encounter with a seemingly autonomous being or entity after a 'breakthrough' dose of DMT, recruited through postings on websites and forums and by email. After exclusions (psychotic disorder diagnosis, other substances, routes other than smoking or vaporizing, duplicates, poor-quality answers) 2561 respondents described their single most memorable encounter: closed questions on senses, communication, labels, emotions, interpretation, comparison with other life experiences and changes they attributed to it (questionnaire adapted from the same group's God-encounter survey), and two open-ended questions on messages and predictions coded by qualitative content analysis. Mixed methods: the quantitative part is appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist and the content analysis is described.
can_establish: What 2561 self-selected English-speaking adults, who had had an entity encounter after inhaled DMT taken without other drugs, reported about their single most memorable encounter, how they interpreted it, and which lasting changes they attributed to it.
cannot_establish: How common entity encounters are among people who use DMT (recruitment required one); anything about whether the entities exist or whether messages and predictions are true (these are unverifiable reports and beliefs); that the experience caused the reported changes in belief, well-being or behaviour (a single retrospective report, no comparison group, 'before' values recalled years later); or the full range of such experiences, including harmful ones (most memorable experience only; people with psychotic disorders and those who used other substances excluded).

sample.recruitment: Postings on websites (for example motherboard.com, facebook.com, reddit.com, dmt-nexus.me, bluelight.org, drugs-forum.com) and email announcements, each linking to an anonymous Qualtrics survey, February to December 2018; approved by the Johns Hopkins School of Medicine institutional review board (p. 1009, Method › Procedure, 1st paragraph; Study recruitment flow, 1st paragraph). Payment is not mentioned.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Inclusion: aged 18 or over; fluent in English; at least one 'breakthrough' dose of DMT, defined as one that produced very strong psychoactive effects; and an encounter with a seemingly autonomous being or entity after DMT (p. 1009). Excluded at consent: previously completed (150), under 18 (50), not fluent in English (103), no breakthrough experience (342), no entity encounter (484). Excluded after completion: prior diagnosis of a psychotic disorder (103), other substances that may have affected the DMT experience (1279), DMT by a route other than smoking or vaporizing (457); then duplicate IP addresses (34) and, on qualitative review, 176 more (63 undisclosed use of other substances, 36 changa, 37 inattentive answers, 40 a combination) (pp. 1009–1010).
sample.demographics: Mean age 31.9 (SD 9.1); mean age at the described experience 27.3 (SD 7.9); 77% male; 85% White, 10% mixed race; 10% Hispanic; 64% living in the USA; 52% never married; 17% high school or less, 30% some college, 17% trade school or associate degree, 26% bachelor's degree, 11% advanced degree; 52% with income of US$35,000 or more (Table 1, p. 1011; Results › Respondent characteristics, 1st paragraph, p. 1010).
sample.attrition: Not a follow-up study. Of 9179 eligible consenters, 4610 (50.2%, editors' calculation) completed the survey and affirmed their answers; non-completers are not described. All percentages are given as shares of the total sample of 2561, and item non-response is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Recruited mainly from DMT-focused and drug-discussion forums and social media, in English. Only people who had an entity encounter were eligible, so the sample says nothing about how often encounters occur. Excluding psychotic disorders, other substance use (1279, 27.7% of completers, editors' calculation), other routes and changa leaves a filtered subset of experiences. Each person reported one 'most memorable' experience, on average about 4.6 years earlier (31.9 minus 27.3 years, editors' calculation from the means). The authors acknowledge that people with life-disrupting experiences may have been less likely to respond (p. 1018, Discussion › Potential harms) and that the sample's representativeness cannot be determined (p. 1018, Discussion › Study limitations).

exposure.measurement: Self-report: a 'breakthrough' dose of vaporized or smoked DMT; lifetime DMT uses (response options up to 101 or more); number of entity encounters before and after the described one. Nothing was tested; the source, purity and amount of DMT and the setting of the experience are not reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Recorded here only as study conditions. Route: smoked or vaporized only (other routes excluded). Amount: none reported beyond the 'breakthrough' criterion (very strong effects). Lifetime DMT uses: median 6 (Table 2); the text gives a mean of 14.5 (SD 22.9) (p. 1010). For 67% the described encounter was their first; 33% had encounters before it (median 3, n=849) and 46% after it (median 3, n=1105) (Table 2, p. 1011).
exposure.polysubstance: Respondents reporting other substances that may have affected the experience were excluded (1279 at eligibility and 63 more on qualitative review), as were those who used changa (36). Use of other drugs at other times is not reported.

comparison.controls: None within the study. The Discussion compares the results with the authors' earlier survey of God-encounter experiences (Griffiths et al., 2019), reporting higher ratings there (t-tests, p<0.001, no statistics given) (p. 1014), and with descriptions of non-drug alien-abduction, near-death and religious experiences from the literature (pp. 1016–1017).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Religious or spiritual beliefs, well-being, life satisfaction and personality before the experience were not measured at the time; religious identification 'before' was recalled in the same sitting as 'after'. Expectations, setting and company during the experience were not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Study questionnaire modified from the God-encounter survey (Griffiths et al., 2019); the full questionnaire is in an online supplement that was not among the files. Closed items: intention, who initiated the encounter, senses, communication and its mode, descriptive labels, the respondent's and the entity's emotions (all that apply and the most prominent), clarity of memory (0–100), familiarity (0–4), how real during and after (0–100), where the entity existed, attributes (rated moderately or more), change in conception of reality, religious identification before and after, comparison with other lifetime experiences (1–8) and persisting changes attributed to the experience (−3 to +3) (Tables 3–5). Two open-ended questions on any message, task, mission, purpose or insight, and on any prediction about the future (p. 1010, Method › Entity survey).
outcomes.validity_norms: No psychometric validation is reported. Open-ended answers were coded by the first three authors in a content analysis; a random 20% of responses to each item was coded independently by an author not involved in coding, with 95% agreement for prediction themes and 94% for message themes (percentage agreement, no chance-corrected statistic) (p. 1010, Data analyses › Analytic plan).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Enduring effects' and 'persisting changes' are respondents' ratings of change that they attribute to the experience (any rating of +1 to +3 counted as a positive change); change in worldview is the share endorsing items about reality and the entity; change in religious identification compares recalled and current identification reported at the same time.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Bonferroni correction for the four before–after comparisons of religious identification (z-tests for dependent proportions; Table 4 footnote, p. 1013). The comparisons with the God-encounter survey (several t-tests) are reported only as p<0.001, without the number of tests or any correction (p. 1014). Everything else is descriptive.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable for closed items; the coders of open-ended answers were authors and not blind.

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive percentages of the total sample, without intervals; with 2561 respondents a 95% interval is at most about plus or minus 2 percentage points (editors' calculation; for example 69% reporting a message, Wilson 67.4% to 71.0%). Religious identification, recalled before vs current: atheist 28% vs 10%; agnostic 27% vs 16%; belief in ultimate reality, higher power, God or universal divinity 36% vs 58%; other 9% vs 16%; each p<0.001 by z-test for dependent proportions with Bonferroni correction; no test statistics or cross-tabulation of individual changes are printed (Table 4, p. 1013).
analysis.selective_reporting: Negative changes attributed to the experience are given only as a range (1–5%) in the text, not per domain. The comparison with the God-encounter survey is reported only as 't-tests, p<0.001', and the authors say a full statistical comparison was beyond their scope (p. 1014). The questionnaire wording is only in the supplement.
analysis.power: Not applicable to the descriptive aims; not reported.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 2561 self-selected adults who had had an entity encounter after inhaled DMT taken without other drugs, reporting on their most memorable one about 4.6 years later on average: vision (92%) and extrasensory contact (85%) dominated; 84% reported communication, 40% two-way; the labels were mostly generic (being 60%, guide 43%, spirit 39%, alien 39%, helper 34%). Love, joy and kindness were the commonest emotions, but 41% felt fear at some point and 32% rated the experience among their five most psychologically challenging. Respondents described the entity as conscious (96%), intelligent (96%) and benevolent (78%); 72% believed it continued to exist afterwards and 75% placed it at least partly in another real dimension; 69% reported receiving a message and 19% a prediction. Recalled atheism fell from 28% to 10%. Most attributed positive lasting changes to the experience (well-being 89%), and 1–5% negative changes.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that aspects of the experience and its interpretation “produced profound and enduring ontological changes in worldview” (p. 1008), and the Discussion says the survey “provides strong evidence of such changes” (p. 1017), while the limitations state that the cross-sectional design “makes causal interpretations impossible” (p. 1018). Gaps: (1) the before–after change in religious identification compares a recalled past with the present, in one sitting, years after the event, in people recruited because they had the experience; (2) the 'enduring effects' are respondents' attributions, not measured change, with no comparison group; (3) the suggestions that such experiences may have therapeutic potential (pp. 1017–1018, Discussion › Ascertaining messages or predictions about the future, 1st paragraph) and that DMT could show promise as an adjunct to therapy for depression and addiction (p. 1018, Conclusion) extrapolate from self-attributed insight; (4) the conclusion that DMT encounters resemble religious, alien-abduction and near-death experiences rests on comparisons with published descriptions, not on data collected in parallel. On the reality of the entities the paper is careful: it reports beliefs and calls the predictions unverifiable (p. 1018). A headline saying that people on DMT meet real beings, or that DMT turns atheists into believers, would overstate the study: what was measured is what self-selected people who had such an experience later said they believed about it.

timeline.event: Strassman, describing his studies of high-dose intravenous DMT, estimated that at least half of participants reported journeys to other worlds, with contact with beings or entities as a variant; read here only as cited (p. 1009).

Cott and Rock, thematic analysis of DMT experiences in 19 self-selected people, including reports of entering other realities sometimes inhabited by sentient beings; read here only as cited (p. 1009).

Griffiths et al., online survey of God-encounter experiences, naturally occurring or after psilocybin, LSD, ayahuasca or DMT (PLoS One 14: e0214377), the source of this questionnaire and the main comparison in the Discussion; read here only as cited (pp. 1009–1010, 1014).

replication.where_it_stands: By its authors' account the largest survey to date of DMT entity encounters (p. 1018). Its numbers describe a filtered, self-selected group's reports and beliefs. The authors name the prevalence of entity encounters among people who use DMT, and how consistently they recur across occasions, as questions for future studies (p. 1018); controlled laboratory studies are proposed in the Conclusion but none is reported here.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective measurement of beliefs, well-being and religious identification before and after DMT given under controlled conditions, ideally with an active placebo and blinded assessment and follow-up over months, together with a survey of people who use DMT recruited regardless of whether they had an encounter, recording how often encounters happen across occasions. Whether the entities exist is not a question a survey can settle.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: No frame: recruitment through DMT-related and drug-discussion websites, social media and email.
Self-selected volunteers; eligibility required an entity encounter, and large groups were excluded after completion (other substances, psychotic disorder, other routes).
2561 respondents give shares precise to about plus or minus 2 percentage points (editors' calculation).

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Demographics and DMT history are described (Tables 1–2), but nothing about the setting, amount or source of the DMT, and time since the experience only through the two mean ages.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Only 4610 of 9179 eligible consenters completed, and 2049 completers were then excluded by design or for data quality; item non-response is not reported, and shares of the total sample may mix 'no' with missing answers.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Study-specific, unvalidated questionnaire; retrospective recall of the most memorable experience years earlier; 'before' religious identification recalled at the same time as 'after'; lasting changes are attributions rather than measured change.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants
domains.note: The same online questionnaire for everyone; open-ended coding with 94–95% agreement on a 20% subsample (percentage agreement only); no test–retest reliability.
Descriptive percentages suit the aim, but no intervals, no cross-tabulation behind the before–after identification tests, and the comparison with the God-encounter survey is reported only as p<0.001.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response managed
domains.note: No denominator of people reached; of 9179 eligible consenters only 4610 (50%) completed, and non-completers are not compared with completers.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist (editors' summary: high risk of bias) because the encyclopedia will use shares of respondents reporting each feature. The shares are precise for this sample but describe a doubly selected group: people from DMT-oriented online communities who had an entity encounter, used no other drug at the time, and completed a 39-minute survey, recalling their most memorable experience years later. The qualitative content analysis is described (method, coders, 20% double-coded with 94–95% agreement) but not appraised as a separate study. The source may be cited for what these respondents reported and believed about their experiences; not for how often encounters happen among people who use DMT, for causal effects on belief or well-being, or for anything about the reality of the entities.

key_findings.finding: Recruitment, February–December 2018: 20,340 people clicked a study link and 10,308 consented; 1129 were excluded at consent (150 had already completed the survey, 50 were under 18, 103 were not fluent in English, 342 had no breakthrough DMT experience, 484 had not encountered an entity), leaving 9179 eligible, of whom 4610 completed the survey and affirmed their answers were accurate.

key_findings.finding: Of the 4610, 1839 were excluded by design (103 prior diagnosis of a psychotic disorder, 1279 other substances that may have affected the DMT experience, 457 a route other than smoking or vaporizing); 34 more for duplicate IP addresses and 176 after qualitative review (63 undisclosed use of other substances, 36 changa, 37 inattentive answers, 40 a combination). Mean completion time was 39 min and no one was removed for fast responding; the final sample was 2561.
key_findings.locator: Method › Study recruitment flow, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (the 2nd continuing on p. 1010)

key_findings.finding: Respondents: mean age 31.9 (SD 9.1), mean age at the described experience 27.3 (SD 7.9); 77% male; 85% White; 64% living in the USA; 52% never married; 52% with income of US$35,000 or more.
key_findings.locator: Results › Respondent characteristics, 1st paragraph (p. 1010); Table 1 (p. 1011)
key_findings.note: The two mean ages imply that the described experience happened on average about 4.6 years before the survey (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Lifetime DMT use: median 6 occasions (the text gives a mean of 14.5, SD 22.9). For 67% the described encounter was their first DMT entity encounter; 33% had had encounters before it (median 3, n=849) and 46% after it (median 3, n=1105); 56% before or after.
key_findings.locator: Results › Respondent characteristics, 1st paragraph (p. 1010); Table 2 (p. 1011)

key_findings.finding: Features of the encounter: 21% had intended to have one; 69% said the entity initiated it (7% that they did). Senses: vision 92%, extrasensory (for example telepathic) 85%, hearing 54%, touch 34%, smell 9%, taste 6%. 84% reported communication: 40% two-way, 49% one-way from the entity, 2% one-way from the respondent; mostly by telepathy (74%), gestures (40%) or spoken language (26%).

key_findings.note: The remaining 24% for who initiated the encounter is not described.

key_findings.finding: Labels respondents chose for the entity (all that apply): being 60%, guide 43%, spirit 39%, alien 39%, helper 34%, angel 16%, elf 14%, religious personage 11%, plant spirit 10%, fairy 8%, chemical spirit 8%, animal spirit 7%, clown 6%, demon 6%, gnome 5%, monster 3%, deceased family member 2%, devil 2%, unknown deceased person 2%, deceased friend 1%, other 29%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Details of the most memorable entity encounter, 2nd paragraph (p. 1010); Table 3 (p. 1011)

key_findings.finding: Emotions: 99% reported an emotional response; during the encounter respondents felt joy (65%), trust (63%), surprise (61%), love (59%), kindness (56%), friendship (48%) and fear (41%), less often sadness (13%), distrust (10%), disgust (4%) or anger (3%); love was most often the single most prominent emotion (21%). 58% said the entity also seemed to have an emotional response, most prominently love (17%), kindness (11%) or joy (10%), with negative emotions at 2% or less.

key_findings.finding: Respondents rated the encounter as more real than everyday waking consciousness as it felt during the experience (81%) and as it seems now (65%) (mean 77.3, SD 29.7, and 63.2, SD 34.4, on a 0–100 scale where 100 means more real than everyday reality). From their current perspective, 49% said the entity existed in some real but different dimension or reality, 26% there and in everyday physical reality, 9% completely within themselves, 1% only in everyday reality, 15% other; 72% believed it continued to exist after the encounter.
key_findings.locator: Results › Additional details of the most memorable encounter experience and its interpretation having metaphysical implications, 1st paragraph (p. 1012, continuing in the right column); Table 4 (p. 1013)
key_findings.note: Beliefs reported by respondents, not findings about the entities. Familiarity of the experience averaged 1.2 (SD 1.4) on a 0–4 scale (0 = not at all familiar), and clarity of the memory 59.9 (SD 31.6) on a 0–100 scale from not very clear to completely clear.

key_findings.finding: 80% said the experience altered their fundamental conception of reality: 60% of the whole sample called the alteration desirable, 1% undesirable and 19% neither.
key_findings.locator: Results › Additional details …, 1st paragraph (p. 1012, right column); Table 4 (p. 1013)

key_findings.finding: Attributes respondents gave the entity (rated moderately or more): conscious 96%, intelligent 96%, benevolent 78%, sacred 70%, had agency in the world 54%, positively judgmental 52%, eternal 42%, all-knowing 38%, petition-able 23%, negatively judgmental 16%, malicious 11%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Additional details …, 2nd paragraph (p. 1012); Table 4 (p. 1013)

key_findings.finding: Religious identification recalled for before the encounter vs reported for after it: atheist 28% vs 10%; agnostic 27% vs 16%; belief in ultimate reality, higher power, God or universal divinity 36% vs 58%; other 9% vs 16%; each change p<0.001 (z-tests for dependent proportions, Bonferroni-corrected).
key_findings.locator: Results › Additional details …, 3rd paragraph (p. 1012); Table 4 and footnote f (p. 1013)
key_findings.note: Both values were given in one sitting, the 'before' value by recall years later. By the editors' arithmetic the fall from 28% to 10% means that at least 64% of those who recalled being atheist no longer identified as atheist, which is consistent with the abstract's 'more than half'; the paper prints no cross-tabulation.

key_findings.finding: Compared with other lifetime experiences (1–8 scale; 7 = among the five most, 8 = the single most), mean ratings were 6.3 (SD 1.4) for personal meaning, 6.5 (1.7) spiritual significance, 6.0 (1.9) psychological insight and 4.6 (2.5) psychological challenge; among the top five or the single most: 55%, 65%, 54% and 32%; the single most: 16%, 31%, 20% and 11%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Comparison to other lifetime experiences and persisting changes attributed to the experience, 1st paragraph (p. 1012); Table 5 (p. 1014)

key_findings.finding: Changes respondents attributed to the experience (−3 to +3; share rating any positive, desirable change): well-being or life satisfaction mean 2.0 (SD 1.1), 89%; life's purpose 1.8 (1.2), 82%; life's meaning 1.8 (1.2), 81%; social relationships 1.4 (1.3), 70%; attitudes about life 2.0 (1.1), 88%; attitudes about self 1.9 (1.2), 84%; mood 1.4 (1.3), 67%; behaviour 1.4 (1.2), 71%; spirituality 1.8 (1.2), 80%; attitudes about death 1.8 (1.3), 76%. The Results text states that only 1–5% reported negative, undesirable changes in the eight domains it lists (well-being to behaviour); spirituality and attitudes about death are not in that list.
key_findings.locator: Results › Comparison to other lifetime experiences and persisting changes attributed to the experience, 1st paragraph (p. 1012); Table 5 (p. 1014)
key_findings.note: Self-attributed changes reported once, with no measurement before the experience and no comparison group. The negative percentages are given only as a range in the text.

key_findings.finding: 69% (1773 of 2561) said they received a message, task, mission, purpose or insight. Themes as shares of the whole sample: idiosyncratic information 703 (27%), personal insight 571 (22%), love 409 (16%), task 280 (11%), safety/reassurance 259 (10%), interconnectedness 180 (7%), death 168 (7%), knowledge 161 (6%), greeting, farewell or reprimand 104 (4%), prediction 99 (4%), divinity 66 (3%), DMT space more real than everyday reality 52 (2%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Ascertaining a message and predictions about the future, 1st paragraph (p. 1012, continuing on p. 1013); Table 6 (p. 1015)

key_findings.finding: 19% (484 of 2561) said they received a prediction about the future. Themes as shares of the whole sample: personal life event 156 (6%), transpersonal, interdimensional or extraterrestrial event 64, negative state of the world 63 (2%), idiosyncratic prediction 62 (2%), afterlife 54 (2%), positive state of the world 33 (1%), safety/reassurance 32 (1%), dying or timing of death 26 (1%), meeting the entity again 19 (1%). The authors state such predictions are unverifiable with this method in anonymous respondents.
key_findings.locator: Results › Ascertaining a message and predictions about the future, 2nd paragraph (p. 1013, continuing on p. 1014); Table 7 (p. 1016); Discussion › Ascertaining messages or predictions about the future, 2nd paragraph (p. 1018)
key_findings.note: The transpersonal theme is printed as 3% in Table 7 and 2% in the text; 64 of 2561 is 2.5% (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Fear and challenge: 41% felt fear during the encounter, and 32% rated it among the five most psychologically challenging experiences of their lives, although fear was rarely the most prominent emotion (7%).
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (continued, p. 1012); Table 5 (p. 1014); Discussion › Positive and negative emotional responses during the encounter, 1st paragraph (p. 1017)
key_findings.note: The same Discussion paragraph gives distrust as 19%, while Table 3 and the Results give 10% (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Potential harms: the authors note that only 1–5% reported enduring negative attributions, then point to potential harms that the survey did not examine: harmful attributions may have been underestimated, because people with life-disrupting experiences may have been less likely to respond, and harm may have gone undetected because respondents described only their most memorable experience; the shifts in religious identification and in worldview may be seen as positive by some and negative by others, and changed beliefs might lead to physical, psychological or epistemic harm; and future research should assess whether such beliefs predispose to self-destructive behaviour or signal the onset of psychotic illness. They say the study provided no evidence of such harmful outcomes, which the survey did not examine.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Potential harms, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Not a finding of no harm: the harms named lie outside what the survey measured, as the paragraph itself states.

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: retrospective recall and social desirability bias; a cross-sectional design that makes causal interpretation impossible and cannot show whether the sample represents people who use DMT; exclusions for other substances, changa and non-inhaled routes; and reports limited to the most memorable experience.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Study limitations, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors compare their results with their earlier God-encounter survey (Griffiths et al., 2019): similar demographics and many similar response patterns, with ratings of personal meaning, spiritual significance and positive lasting effects significantly higher in the God-encounter survey (t-tests, p<0.001); the descriptors God, ultimate reality and higher power were not offered as labels in the present survey.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Similarities of DMT entity encounter experiences to DMT God/ultimate reality encounter experiences, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 1014, the 3rd continuing on p. 1016)
key_findings.note: No test statistics, means or sample sizes are printed for the comparison.

key_findings.finding: Background stated in the introduction from cited sources, not from this survey: DMT has been found in the mammalian brain, and it has been speculated to play a role in dreaming, psychosis, spiritual and near-death experiences, but it is not clear that it occurs in the body in concentrations sufficient to have pharmacological effects.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand: cited to Barker (2018) and Nichols (2018), among others; not read for this card.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says 41% and 19% of respondents felt fear and distrust during the encounter; Table 3 and the Results text give distrust as 10%.
reporting_issues.consequence: The distrust figure appears in two versions; the table value (10%) should be used.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 7 prints the transpersonal, interdimensional or extraterrestrial theme as 64 (3%), while the Results text gives it as 2%.
reporting_issues.consequence: 64 of 2561 is 2.5% (editors' calculation), so the two values are a rounding inconsistency; quote the count.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says 22% of 'these responses' (the messages reported by 69%) involved a personal insight; 22% is the share of the whole sample (571 of 2561).
reporting_issues.consequence: Among the 1773 who reported a message, the share is about 32% (editors' calculation); the denominator should be stated with either figure.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives 46% as having entity encounters after the described one, but the number of such encounters is summarized for n=1105.
reporting_issues.consequence: By the editors' arithmetic 46% of 2561 is about 1178, so about 70 respondents may lack a count, or one of the two figures is wrong; not explained.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 reports communication with the entity for 84%, but by the editors' addition the three types of communication sum to 91%; its footnote says the questions were separate and the differences reflect actual survey data. Likewise, the entity's most prominent emotions add up to about 70% of the sample while 58% said the entity had an emotional response.
reporting_issues.consequence: Answers to linked questions are not consistent; shares from these items should be quoted as printed, with their question, not combined.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion lists, among similarities with the God-encounter survey, that about 80% reported communication described as a two-way exchange; in this survey 84% reported any communication and 40% two-way communication.
reporting_issues.consequence: The parenthetical misdescribes this survey's result; two-way communication was reported by 40%.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives a mean of 14.5 lifetime DMT uses (SD 22.9) citing Table 2, which reports only the median (6) on a scale whose top option was 101 or more.
reporting_issues.consequence: A mean from a capped category scale understates the spread and is driven by the few people who used DMT very often; the median is the better summary.

reporting_issues.issue: The comparison with the God-encounter survey is reported only as 't-tests, p<0.001', with no means, test statistics, sample sizes or number of tests, and the authors say a full statistical comparison was beyond the scope of the paper.
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim that the God-encounter experiences were rated higher cannot be checked or weighed from this paper.
