design_detail: Anonymous, unpaid online survey (Qualtrics; about 50 minutes in one sitting) from Johns Hopkins, recruiting through internet advertisements, email invitations and online social networks between dates printed as 12/03/2014 and 08/01/2016. Two versions: one for people who had what they took to be an encounter with God, a Higher Power, Ultimate Reality or an aspect or emissary of God after taking a classic psychedelic (Psychedelic Group), one for people who had such an experience without any psychoactive drug and never after one (Non-Drug Group). Respondents described their single most memorable encounter: study-made closed items on its details, interpretation, comparison with other lifetime experiences, persisting changes they attributed to it and religious identification immediately before and after it (both rated at the survey), plus the Mystical Experience Questionnaire (MEQ30). 4285 usable responses: Non-Drug 809; psilocybin 1184, LSD 1251, ayahuasca 435 and DMT other than ayahuasca 606 (combined Psychedelic Group 3476). Groups were compared with general linear models (logit link for proportions) and ANOVA adjusted for eight dichotomized demographic covariates, with Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise tests and p≤0.001 as threshold. Appraised as a survey; the group comparisons are descriptive and confounded (see comparison).
can_establish: What self-selected English-speaking adults who had a God encounter experience reported about their single most memorable one, and how the reports of those whose experience followed psilocybin, LSD, ayahuasca or DMT compared descriptively with those whose experience occurred without drugs.
cannot_establish: How often such experiences occur with or without psychedelics (only people who had one were recruited); whether psychedelics cause the experiences, their features or the changes attributed to them (no measures before the experience, no comparison with people who did not have one); whether differences between groups reflect the drug rather than who answered each version (the groups differed in age, sex, education, country and, by recall, religion before the experience, which was not adjusted for); or the reality of what was encountered, which the authors say descriptive studies cannot address (p. 22).

sample.recruitment: Internet advertisements, email invitations and online social networks linking to the version of the questionnaire for each group; anonymous; no compensation; approved by the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine institutional review board (p. 3, Methods › Participant recruitment; Survey administration). The sites and lists used are not named. Recruitment dates printed as 12/03/2014–08/01/2016 (p. 5, Results › Survey completion).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Both versions: at least 18 years old; fluent in English; not completed before. Psychedelic version: a God encounter after a dose of a classic hallucinogen with moderate to strong psychoactive effects. Non-Drug version: a God encounter, and never one after taking a psychoactive drug (p. 4, Methods › Inclusion criteria, 1st paragraph). Of 12,725 who began: 1702 did not meet the criteria, 5165 did not complete, 401 reported multiple substances, 602 a substance other than psilocybin, LSD, ayahuasca or DMT, 271 answered about several experiences, 104 gave answers of doubtful validity, 34 asked not to be included and 161 had nonsystematic coding errors, leaving 4285 (p. 5; the exclusions add up exactly, editors' check). Analysis of the psychedelic version was restricted to the four drug categories (p. 4).
sample.demographics: All respondents: mean age 38.3 at the survey and 27.2 at the experience, which happened on average 11.0 years earlier; 69% male; 88% White; 48% with a college or graduate degree (p. 5). Non-Drug vs Psychedelic Group: age 56.2 (SD 13.7) vs 34.1 (12.8); age at the experience 35.7 (15.0) vs 25.3 (9.1); years since the experience 20.5 (15.4) vs 8.8 (10.6); male 27% vs 79%; White 93% vs 86%; Black or African American 1% in both; US residents 75% vs 59%; ever married 76% vs 46% (Table 1, p. 6). DMT Group: age 30.0 (8.3), experience 4.7 (3.3) years earlier, 82% male, 33% with a bachelor's degree or higher, 63% US residents (Table 2, p. 7); the group consisted mainly of people who smoked DMT, with 3 of 606 commenting in ways suggesting a nasal route (p. 7).
sample.attrition: Not a follow-up study. 5165 of the 11,023 who met the criteria (47%, editors' calculation) did not complete the questionnaire; 82% of them did not complete a quarter of the items and 93% did not complete half (p. 5). Non-completers are not described and item non-response is not reported. 67% wrote an open-ended comment; median completion time 50 minutes (p. 5).
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected volunteers who chose to describe a God encounter; the survey's stated purpose named God, a Higher Power, Ultimate Reality and emissaries of God, which favours religious or spiritual interpretations. The two groups were recruited into different versions and differ in age, sex, education, income, country and, by recall, religious identification before the experience (monotheist 47% vs 12%; atheist 3% vs 21%; Table 13, p. 18). Only 1% were Black or African American (p. 23). Each person described a single most memorable experience, on average 20.5 years earlier in the Non-Drug Group. Experiences after several substances were excluded. The authors say they do not know how representative the samples are and that the long, unpaid, anonymous survey may have contributed to selection bias (p. 23). The sample cannot represent how often God encounters happen to people who use psychedelics or to anyone else, typical rather than memorable experiences, or people who do not read English.

exposure.measurement: Self-report: the substance respondents believed they had taken (psilocybin mushrooms or psilocybin, LSD, ayahuasca, or DMT other than ayahuasca; mescaline, peyote and other substances were not analysed) (pp. 4–5). Nothing was verified; amount, setting and company, other than whether the person was alone, were not recorded, and the authors note that detailed information on the context of use was not obtained (p. 20).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Recorded here only as study conditions: one experience after a dose with moderate to strong psychoactive effects (inclusion criterion); amount not recorded. DMT outside ayahuasca was mostly smoked; ayahuasca is drunk (pp. 7, 21).
exposure.polysubstance: Respondents who indicated taking multiple substances for the experience (401) were excluded (p. 5); drug use at other times is not reported. The Non-Drug Group excluded anyone who had ever had such an experience after a psychoactive drug; their drug use otherwise is not reported.

comparison.controls: Non-Drug Group (n=809): people describing a God encounter that occurred without drugs. The four psychedelic groups were also compared with each other.
comparison.matching: None. Comparisons were adjusted for eight dichotomized covariates that differed between groups: age at the survey (over 32), age at the experience (over 23), sex, White race, college graduate, US resident, household income over $50,000 a year, and ever married (p. 4, Methods › Statistical analyses, 3rd paragraph, continuing on p. 5).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Religious identification before the experience was recalled at the survey, years later, and was not used as a covariate, although it differed greatly between groups (Table 13). Personality, mental health, expectations, setting, prior spiritual practice and intention (beyond one yes/no item) were not measured or not adjusted.

outcomes.instruments: Study questionnaire in two versions (S2 and S3 Files, not read): intention, who initiated the encounter, being alone, senses involved, communication (any, two-way, one-way, mode), emotional response, message, predictions; vividness of memory and three realism ratings (0–100); best descriptor of what was encountered (God, Ultimate Reality, Higher Power, aspect or emissary of God); 11 attributes (yes, no, I don't know) with degree ratings; three further interpretation items; comparison with other lifetime experiences (1–8, where 7 = among the 5 most and 8 = the single most); nine persisting-change ratings (−3 to +3) and six yes/no change items; religious identification immediately before and after the experience (24 descriptors grouped as atheist, monotheist for Christian, Jewish or Islam, and other). MEQ30 answered for the time of the encounter, with complete mystical experience defined beforehand as at least 60% on all four subscales (p. 4, Methods › Survey description; Tables 3–14).
outcomes.validity_norms: The MEQ30 was developed and validated for psilocybin sessions; the authors suggest its higher scores in the Psychedelic Group may partly reflect that origin (p. 18). Other items are study-made and unvalidated, answered about experiences on average 11 years earlier.
outcomes.operationalization: Persisting changes = respondents' ratings of changes they attribute to the experience; change in religious identification = recalled identification before the experience compared with identification after it, both reported at the survey; complete mystical experience = the MEQ30 criterion.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Group comparisons were considered significant at p≤0.001, with Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise comparisons (pp. 4–5); religious-identification comparisons at Bonferroni-adjusted p≤0.05 (p. 5). The authors count 76 items assessing the details and consequences of the experience (p. 20).

analysis.effect_sizes: Percentages and means (SD) by group, with significance flags from adjusted models; no effect sizes or confidence intervals in the article (estimated means and standard errors are in S1 File, not read). Examples, Non-Drug vs Psychedelic Group: best descriptor God 41% vs 18% and Ultimate Reality 26% vs 55% (Table 7, p. 12); complete mystical experience 43% vs 64% (Table 5, p. 10); atheist before vs after 3% to 1% and 21% to 8% (Table 13, p. 18); of those atheist before, 74% and 67% no longer identified as atheist afterwards, not significantly different (p. 14).
analysis.covariates: Eight dichotomized demographic covariates (see comparison); not prior religion, context of use or time since the experience as such.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned (registries not searched). Data are deposited on the Open Science Framework (osf.io/ykz5w) (p. 1).
analysis.selective_reporting: Degree ratings of attributes are given only in the text, not in tables (p. 10). The Discussion restricts itself to differences with p≤0.001 and more than 10 percentage points (p. 17). The 24 religious descriptors are collapsed into three categories, so it is not shown where people who stopped identifying as atheist went within 'other'.
analysis.power: Not reported; groups of 435 to 1251 give precise estimates within each group.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 4285 self-selected respondents describing their most memorable God encounter, often many years earlier, those whose experience followed a psychedelic and those whose experience occurred without drugs reported broadly similar features: communication (63% and 67%), a message, task or insight (78% and 75%), an emotional response (91% and 88%), attributes such as intelligent, sacred, eternal and conscious, and positive persisting changes they attributed to the experience (means around 2 on a −3 to +3 scale). The Non-Drug Group more often chose God as the best descriptor (41% vs 18%) and was more often alone (58% vs 35%); the Psychedelic Group more often chose Ultimate Reality (55% vs 26%), reported visual (75% vs 48%) and extrasensory (86% vs 64%) involvement, met the complete mystical experience criterion (64% vs 43%) and reported decreased fear of death (70% vs 57%). Recalled atheist identification fell from 3% to 1% and from 21% to 8%, while 'other' identification rose (50% to 59% and 67% to 85%) and, in the Psychedelic Group, monotheist identification fell (12% to 7%).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the encounter met criteria for a complete mystical experience in approximately half of the participants, that more than two-thirds of those atheist before no longer identified as atheist afterwards, and that moderate to strong positive persisting changes were attributed to the experiences (p. 1); the Discussion implies, citing the Principle of Causal Indifference and then calling the descriptions in the two groups markedly similar while acknowledging differences, that drug-occasioned experiences cannot be judged less genuine, and that God versus Ultimate Reality may reflect semantics rather than phenomenology (p. 22); it also suggests that DMT produces a distinct profile of effects (p. 21). Gaps: (1) half fits neither group (43% and 64%; 60% overall by the editors' calculation); (2) the change in identification compares a recalled past with the present, years later, in people recruited for having had the experience, and, by the group margins (individual transitions are not reported), the net shift away from atheism went to 'other', not to a monotheistic tradition; (3) similar self-descriptions in two differently recruited groups do not establish that the experiences are equivalent, and the God versus Ultimate Reality difference may follow the groups' prior religion (47% vs 12% monotheist before), which was not adjusted for; (4) the DMT conclusion rests on comparisons between groups that, as the authors concede, cannot separate pharmacology from expectancy and context (p. 21); (5) persisting changes are attributions, not measured change. The authors state that descriptive data cannot address whether God exists (p. 22). A headline version (psychedelics turn atheists into believers, or psychedelic experiences are the same as religious ones) would overstate.

timeline.event: Yaden et al.: online survey comparing religious, spiritual and mystical experiences that respondents said were or were not influenced by psychedelics (about 330 per group); the psychedelic group attributed greater purpose, spirituality and reduced fear of death to them; as described by this paper (pp. 18, 20), which found few differences in persisting changes; not read.

Davis et al. (2020b): survey of 2561 people who had an entity encounter after inhaled DMT, using a questionnaire modified from this one; similar demographics and many similar response patterns, with lower ratings of meaning, spiritual significance and lasting positive effects than in this survey (project card sc_davis_2020b).

replication.where_it_stands: No direct replication was read. Against the companion card sc_davis_2020b: this paper supplies the numbers behind that survey's comparison, which Davis et al. report only as p<0.001. In this survey's DMT Group (n=606) personal meaning averaged 6.97, spiritual significance 7.14 and attributed change in well-being 2.26, against 6.3, 6.5 and 2.0 in the entity-encounter survey; communication was reported by 80% of the DMT Group but two-way communication by only 28%, which confirms the reporting issue on that card about an 80% two-way figure. The Non-Drug Group shows that communication with a benevolent, intelligent presence, messages and attributed positive changes are also reported for experiences without drugs, so these features are not specific to DMT. Both surveys share the same limits (selection on the experience, recall years later, no measures before the experience); prospective studies of change in religious identification are named by the authors as future work (p. 22).

funding.funder: As printed (pp. 1–2): conduct of the research primarily supported by grants from the Council on Spiritual Practices (CSP) and the Heffter Research Institute (HRI); Roland Griffiths' effort in writing the manuscript partially provided by NIH grant RO1DA03889; Alan Davis supported by NIDA grant T32DA07209. Robert Jesse, convener of CSP, contributed to writing the manuscript. HRI personnel had no role in study design, data collection and analysis, decision to publish or preparation of the manuscript; no such statement is made for CSP.
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed (p. 2): Roland Griffiths is on the Board of Directors of the Heffter Research Institute and Robert Jesse is convener of the Council on Spiritual Practices; the authors state that this does not alter their adherence to PLOS ONE policies on sharing data and materials.
funding.affiliations_note: Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences; Neuroscience); University of California San Diego (Psychology); Council on Spiritual Practices (p. 1). Both funders support psychedelic or spiritual research, and an officer of one co-wrote the paper. Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective studies that measure religious identification, beliefs and well-being before and after experiences, both psychedelic sessions under controlled conditions (ideally with an active placebo) and naturally occurring experiences, together with surveys of people who use psychedelics recruited regardless of whether they had such an experience, to estimate how often encounters occur and whether they change identification. Whether what was encountered exists is not a question such data can settle.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: No frame: internet advertisements, email invitations and online social networks, not named.
Self-selected volunteers; eligibility required a God encounter; the two groups were recruited into separate versions of the questionnaire.
4285 respondents, 435 to 1251 per group.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Demographics are detailed (Tables 1–2), but the amount, setting and context of the experiences were not obtained and the recruitment sources are not named.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: 47% of those who met the criteria did not complete (editors' calculation) and were excluded; item non-response is not reported.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Study-made items; the MEQ30 was validated for recent sessions but was answered here about experiences on average 11 years earlier; religious identification before the experience was recalled; persisting changes are attributions.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants
domains.note: The same online questionnaire within each group, but two versions for the two groups; no reliability data.
Adjusted models with conservative thresholds, but no effect sizes or intervals in the article, dichotomized covariates, and prior religion not adjusted.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response managed
domains.note: No denominator of people reached; non-completers (5165) not described or compared.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist (editors' summary: high risk of bias) because the encyclopedia will use the shares of respondents reporting each feature, belief and attributed change. The shares are precise within each group but describe self-selected people recalling their most memorable God encounter, on average 11 years (Non-Drug Group about 20 years) earlier. The between-group comparisons are confounded by separate recruitment and by prior religion, which no instrument here captures; they are recorded as descriptive. Cite for what these respondents reported, with group and denominator, and for the descriptive similarity between non-drug and psychedelic accounts. Not for how common such experiences are, for drug effects causing them or the attributed changes, for change in religious identification as measured change, or for conclusions about the reality of what was encountered.

key_findings.finding: Flow: 12,725 began the survey; after excluding 1702 who did not meet the criteria, 5165 who did not complete and, by the editors' sum, 1573 for other reasons (multiple substances 401, other substances 602, several experiences 271, doubtful validity 104, asked to be excluded 34, coding errors 161), 4285 gave usable data: Non-Drug 809, psilocybin 1184, LSD 1251, ayahuasca 435, DMT 606. Median completion time 50 minutes.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 1); Results › Survey completion (single paragraph, p. 5)
key_findings.note: The exclusions sum to 1573 and the flow adds up exactly (editors' check).

key_findings.finding: Non-Drug vs Psychedelic Group: age at the survey 56.2 vs 34.1 years; age at the experience 35.7 vs 25.3; years since the experience 20.5 vs 8.8; male 27% vs 79%; White 93% vs 86%; US residents 75% vs 59%; ever married 76% vs 46%; all differences p≤0.001.
key_findings.locator: Results › Participant characteristics, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 5–6); Table 1 (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Details, Non-Drug vs Psychedelic Group: went in intending an encounter 16% vs 22%; alone 58% vs 35%; senses visual 48% vs 75%, auditory 36% vs 49%, tactile 43% vs 48%, extrasensory 64% vs 86% (all but tactile significant); any communication 63% vs 67%, two-way 22% vs 25%; emotional response 91% vs 88%; a message, task, mission or insight 78% vs 75%; predictions about the future 21% vs 24%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Details of the encounter, 1st paragraph (p. 7); Table 3 (p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Memory and mystical features, Non-Drug vs Psychedelic Group: vividness of memory 91.9 vs 76.2 (0–100); rated more real than everyday consciousness 72.7 vs 76.5 (0–100); MEQ30 total 0.70 vs 0.79 of the maximum; complete mystical experience 43% vs 64% (significantly higher in the Psychedelic Group).
key_findings.locator: Results › Memory, realism, and mystical features of the encounter experience, 1st paragraph (p. 7, continuing on p. 8); Table 5 (p. 10)

key_findings.finding: Best descriptor of what was encountered, Non-Drug vs Psychedelic Group: God 41% vs 18%; Ultimate Reality 26% vs 55%; Higher Power 15% vs 19% (not significant); aspect or emissary of God 18% vs 9%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Interpretation of that which was encountered, 1st paragraph (p. 9); Table 7 (p. 12)

key_findings.finding: Attributes endorsed, Non-Drug vs Psychedelic Group: benevolent 86% vs 70%, intelligent 80% vs 78%, sacred 81% vs 71%, conscious 71% vs 68%, eternal 70% vs 70%, all-knowing 66% vs 59%, agency 47% vs 36%, petitionable 32% vs 18%, negatively judgmental 5% vs 6%, malicious 1% vs 9%; existed at least partly in another dimension or reality 68% vs 69%; continued to exist after the encounter 74% vs 65%; the person was completely the same as what was encountered 32% vs 47%. The Non-Drug Group was significantly more likely to endorse benevolence, agency and petitionability and less likely malice.
key_findings.locator: Results › Interpretation of that which was encountered, 2nd paragraph (p. 10); Table 7 (p. 12)

key_findings.finding: Compared with other lifetime experiences, Non-Drug vs Psychedelic Group: among the 5 most personally meaningful 74% vs 78% and the single most 28% vs 27%; among the 5 most spiritually significant 78% vs 83% and the single most 34% vs 42%; among the 5 most psychologically challenging 32% vs 44% and the single most 12% vs 17%; mean challenge rating 4.21 (SD 2.79) vs 5.27 (2.41) on 1–8, with ratings but not shares of insight and challenge significantly higher in the Psychedelic Group.
key_findings.locator: Results › Comparison of encounter experience relative to other lifetime experiences, 1st paragraph (p. 11); Table 9 (p. 14)

key_findings.finding: Persisting changes attributed to the experience (−3 to +3), Non-Drug vs Psychedelic Group: well-being or life satisfaction 2.38 (0.99) vs 2.21 (1.03); life's purpose 2.16 vs 1.97; life's meaning 2.21 vs 1.99; social relationships 1.76 vs 1.67; spiritual awareness in everyday life 2.44 vs 2.16 (the only significant difference); mood 1.54 vs 1.53; behaviour 1.77 vs 1.58. Decreased fear of death 57% vs 70% (significant); increased fear of death 1% vs 3%; undesirable changes in practice or in understanding other traditions 1–2%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Persisting changes attributed to the encounter, 1st paragraph (p. 12, continuing on p. 13); Table 11 (p. 16)

key_findings.finding: Religious identification, rated at the survey for immediately before and after the experience, Non-Drug vs Psychedelic Group: atheist 3% to 1% and 21% to 8% (both significant decreases); monotheist (Christian, Jewish or Islam) 47% to 41% and 12% to 7% (significant decrease only in the Psychedelic Group); other 50% to 59% and 67% to 85% (significant increase only in the Psychedelic Group). Of those atheist before, 74% and 67% no longer identified as atheist afterwards (difference not significant).
key_findings.locator: Results › Changes in identification as atheist and monotheist, 1st paragraph (p. 13, continuing on p. 14); Table 13 (p. 18)
key_findings.note: Counts are not printed; by the editors' arithmetic from the percentages, about 24 Non-Drug and about 730 Psychedelic respondents identified as atheist before.

key_findings.finding: DMT Group (n=606), detail items: intended an encounter 30%; initiated by what was encountered 56%; alone 35%; visual 83%, extrasensory 89%; any communication 80%, two-way 28%, one-way from it 38%, extrasensory-telepathic 75%; message 74%; predictions 21%; vividness of memory 72.9 (SD 24.6); complete mystical experience 73%.
key_findings.locator: Table 4 (p. 9); Table 6 (p. 11)

key_findings.finding: DMT Group (n=606), interpretation and consequences: best descriptor Ultimate Reality 48%, Higher Power 25%, God 16%, emissary 12%; existed partly in another dimension 76%; continued to exist after the encounter 53%; personal meaning 6.97 (SD 1.07) and spiritual significance 7.14 (1.26) on 1–8; among the 5 most psychologically challenging 47%, the single most 18%; attributed change in well-being 2.26 (0.97), life's meaning 2.02 (1.12), social relationships 1.69 (1.25); decreased fear of death 77%; atheist 25% before and 7% after.
key_findings.locator: Table 8 (p. 13); Table 10 (p. 15); Table 12 (p. 17); Table 14 (p. 19)

key_findings.finding: Among the psychedelic groups: psilocybin and LSD did not differ on any of the 76 items; the DMT Group differed from psilocybin and LSD on 16 of 76 items (more intention, encounters initiated by the other, communication, visual or extrasensory communication, benevolent, intelligent, conscious, existing in another dimension but less often continuing to exist afterwards, higher MEQ30 scores and more complete mystical experiences) and from ayahuasca on only a few. The authors state the survey cannot distinguish pharmacological differences from expectancy and context, and consider it plausible that popular beliefs about DMT, with special interest in entity encounters, may have biased people who use DMT toward having such experiences (an expectancy effect on the experience, not a response bias).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Similarities and differences among different psychedelics, paragraphs headed Psilocybin and LSD groups were very similar (p. 20), DMT Group compared to the Ayahuasca Group and DMT Group compared to the psilocybin and LSD groups (p. 21)

key_findings.finding: The Ayahuasca Group was older, more often female, college-educated, married and outside the USA, less often atheist and least often alone (12%); it tended to have the highest rates of endorsing positive attributes and generally the numerically highest ratings of positive attributed changes, significantly above psilocybin and LSD on several. The authors say detailed information about context of use was not obtained, so the extent to which structured religious or spiritual group settings explain these differences cannot be determined.
key_findings.locator: Table 4 (p. 9); Discussion › Similarities and differences among different psychedelics, paragraph headed Ayahuasca Group compared to the other psychedelic groups (p. 20)

key_findings.finding: The authors note that the higher MEQ30 scores in the Psychedelic Group may partly reflect that the questionnaire was developed and validated for psilocybin-occasioned experiences.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Similarities and differences between Non-Drug and psychedelic-occasioned experiences, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors state that descriptive studies of such experiences cannot definitively address claims about the existence of God.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Can psychedelic drugs occasion genuine God encounter experiences?, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: retrospective self-report, often years later (on average over a decade), open to social desirability and to memories changing over time; a long, unpaid, anonymous survey that may have selected the sample; unknown representativeness; only 1% Black or African American in both groups.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Study strengths and limitations (single paragraph, p. 22, continuing on p. 23)

key_findings.finding: DMT Group realism: 'more real than everyday normal consciousness' was rated a mean 77.5 (SD 32.2) on a 0–100 scale, not significantly different from the Non-Drug Group's 72.7; no share is reported, so a statement that at least 65% in both surveys rated the experience more real cannot be checked against this paper.
key_findings.locator: Table 6 (p. 11)

key_findings.finding: DMT against Ayahuasca Group, communication: the DMT Group more often reported one-way communication from what was encountered (38% vs 22%) and less often two-way communication (28% vs 40%).
key_findings.locator: Table 4 (p. 9); Discussion, paragraph on the DMT Group (p. 21)

key_findings.finding: Some differences flagged as significant: vividness was rated higher in the Non-Drug Group (91.9 vs 76.2; DMT 72.9 also significantly lower); 'completely the same as that which was encountered' (32% vs 47%) and 'initiated by that which was encountered' (55% vs 45%) differed significantly.
key_findings.locator: Tables 3, 5, 6 and 7

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract, Conclusions and Fig 1 say the experience met complete mystical experience criteria in approximately half of the participants; Table 5 gives 43% (Non-Drug) and 64% (Psychedelic), 60% of all respondents by the editors' calculation.
reporting_issues.consequence: Quote the group figures; half fits neither group.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says about one-third rated the experience among the five most psychologically challenging of their lives; Table 9 gives 32% (Non-Drug) and 44% (Psychedelic), 42% overall by the editors' calculation, and 47% in the DMT Group (Table 10).
reporting_issues.consequence: The summary understates challenge in the psychedelic groups; the single most challenging figure (about 15%; 12% and 17% in Table 9) is consistent.

reporting_issues.issue: Fig 1 gives more than 70% for vivid memories and for experiences more real than everyday consciousness, and its legend presents such values as approximate percentages of participants; in Table 5 these are mean ratings on 0–100 scales (vividness 91.9 and 76.2; more real 72.7 and 76.5).
reporting_issues.consequence: The share of respondents rating the experience as more real is not reported; the figure should not be quoted as a percentage of people.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's more than two-thirds of former atheists rests, by the editors' calculation from the percentages in Table 13, on 74% of about 24 Non-Drug respondents and 67% of about 730 Psychedelic respondents who identified as atheist before; the counts are not printed.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure is precise for the Psychedelic Group but rests on about two dozen people in the Non-Drug Group.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say more than 74% of both groups rated the experience among their five most meaningful and spiritually significant; the Non-Drug share for personal meaning is exactly 74% (Table 9).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor wording slip.

reporting_issues.issue: The footnote to Tables 11 and 12 describing the persisting-change scale is garbled (from −3 to +2, and +3), and the degree ratings of attributes (means of 87 and 77 for positively judgmental) are given only in the text, without SDs.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the scale runs from −3 to +3 as in the table headings.

disagreements.first_pass: The abstract says the encounter met criteria for a complete mystical experience in approximately half of the participants, that more than two-thirds of those atheist before no longer identified as atheist afterwards, and that moderate to strong positive persisting changes were attributed to the experiences (p. 1); the Discussion argues that, because descriptions in the two groups are markedly similar, drug-occasioned experiences cannot be judged less genuine, and that God versus Ultimate Reality may reflect semantics rather than phenomenology (p. 22); it also suggests that DMT produces a distinct profile of effects (p. 21). Gaps: (1) half fits neither group (43% and 64%; 60% overall by the editors' calculation); (2) the change in identification compares a recalled past with the present, years later, in people recruited for having had the experience, and leaving atheism mostly meant moving to 'other', not to a monotheistic tradition; (3) similar self-descriptions in two differently recruited groups do not establish that the experiences are equivalent, and the God versus Ultimate Reality difference may follow the groups' prior religion (47% vs 12% monotheist before), which was not adjusted for; (4) the DMT conclusion rests on comparisons between groups that, as the authors concede, cannot separate pharmacology from expectancy and context (p. 21); (5) persisting changes are attributions, not measured change. The authors state that descriptive data cannot address whether God exists (p. 22). A headline version (psychedelics turn atheists into believers, or psychedelic experiences are the same as religious ones) would overstate.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 598 (round-2 check): the authors only imply the 'not less genuine' argument (p. 22); the move from atheism to 'other' is a net shift in group margins, individual transitions not reported.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted by the AI co-editor (adjudication, 13 November 2026): both wording points applied.
